eras.name: Scaling
eras.background: Researchers found that language model loss falls smoothly as models, data and compute grow. That made scale a plan rather than a gamble, and models grew enormously in a few years.

eras.name: Alignment
eras.background: Large pretrained models knew a lot but did not reliably follow instructions. Post-training on human demonstrations and preferences turned them into assistants, and ChatGPT made them a mass-market product.

eras.name: Open weights
eras.background: Frontier labs stopped publishing details, while open-weight models let anyone study, fine-tune and run an LLM. Efficiency techniques such as mixture of experts narrowed the gap to closed models.

eras.name: Reasoning
eras.background: Answering in one pass limited models on math and code. Reinforcement learning taught them to reason at length first, so accuracy grew with inference compute, first in closed and then in open models.

eras.name: Agents
eras.background: Models moved from answering questions to carrying out long tasks: planning, calling tools and editing code. That put pressure on context length and inference cost, driving new attention designs.

nodes.label: Scaling laws
nodes.problem: It was unclear how to split a training budget between model size and data.
nodes.idea: Measure how loss falls as a power law in parameters, data and compute.
nodes.impact: Made model quality predictable and justified training far larger models.

nodes.label: GPT-3
nodes.idea: Scale a language model far up and show it a few examples in the prompt.
nodes.impact: Prompting became the main way to use a language model.

from.why: Loss kept falling predictably with size, so a far larger model was worth training.

nodes.label: InstructGPT
nodes.idea: Fine-tune on demonstrations, train a reward model on human rankings, then optimize with RL.
nodes.impact: RLHF became the standard post-training recipe.

from.why: GPT-3 often ignored instructions or produced untruthful and toxic text.

nodes.label: ChatGPT
nodes.idea: Serve an RLHF-tuned model as a free chat interface.
nodes.impact: Reached a mass audience and set off the race to build assistants.

from.why: Instruction-tuned models were only available to developers through an API.

nodes.label: LLaMA
nodes.idea: Train smaller models on more public data and release the weights to researchers.
nodes.impact: The weights spread widely and seeded open fine-tunes and local inference.

from.why: The strongest models were closed, so few could study or adapt them.

nodes.label: DeepSeek-V3
nodes.idea: Mixture of experts, latent attention and FP8 training cut the cost of a frontier-scale model.
nodes.impact: An open model matched closed ones, and mixture of experts became the default.

from.why: Open models trailed closed ones, and frontier-quality training looked too costly.

nodes.label: o1
nodes.idea: Train with RL to reason at length before answering.
nodes.impact: Thinking time became a second way, besides model size, to buy accuracy.

from.why: Chat models answered at once and failed on multi-step math and code.

nodes.label: DeepSeek-R1
nodes.idea: Apply RL on automatically checkable answers to DeepSeek-V3 and publish the recipe.
nodes.impact: An open recipe for reasoning that other labs quickly adopted.

from.why: o1 showed that RL for reasoning works but kept its method secret.
Supplied a strong open base model to train with RL.

nodes.label: Kimi K2
nodes.idea: Train on synthesized tool-use tasks, then refine with RL.
nodes.impact: Open models became practical as coding and tool-using agents.

from.why: Reasoning models could solve problems but not carry out long tasks with tools.

nodes.label: DeepSeek-V4
nodes.idea: Compress and sparsify attention to handle million-token contexts.
nodes.impact: Long context became affordable in open models.

from.why: Attention cost grows with context length, which limits long agent sessions.

main.title: Stanford CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch
main.why: Tokenizers, Transformer architectures and mixture of experts, GPU kernels and parallelism, scaling laws, inference, data, and post-training with RL. In English.

main.title: The Smol Training Playbook: The Secrets to Building World-Class LLMs
main.why: Papers give the final recipe but hide the decisions, so this playbook walks through SmolLM3's ablations, architecture, data mixture, infrastructure, loss spikes and post-training.

main.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
main.why: Language model loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute, which predicts how to spend a training budget.
Fine-tuning needs labeled data for every task, and GPT-3 shows a large enough model learns tasks from examples in the prompt.

main.title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
main.why: Large models of the time were undertrained, so Chinchilla scales parameters and training tokens equally for a given compute budget.

main.title: Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback
main.why: Pretrained models follow instructions poorly, so InstructGPT adds supervised fine-tuning, a reward model and RLHF.
Inference cost favors smaller models, so LLaMA trains them on more public data than compute-optimal to match much larger ones.
Frontier-scale training was prohibitively expensive, and DeepSeek-V3 reaches that quality cheaply with mixture of experts, latent attention and FP8 training.

background.title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer

main.title: Learning to Reason with LLMs
main.why: OpenAI's o1 is trained with RL to think before answering, and its accuracy grows with both training compute and thinking time.

main.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
main.why: Human-written reasoning data is costly, so DeepSeek-R1 learns long chains of thought from RL on verifiable rewards.

background.title: DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models

further.title: Qwen3 Technical Report
further.why: Thinking is wasted on simple questions, so Qwen3 puts thinking and non-thinking modes in one model with a budget for thinking tokens.

main.title: CMU 11-768: AI Agents
main.why: Tool use, context management, skills and memory, planning, coding and computer-use agents, SFT and RL for agents, sandboxing, multi-agent interaction and search. In English.

main.title: Kimi K2: Open Agentic Intelligence
main.why: Muon trains efficiently but grew unstable at scale, so Kimi K2 adds QK-clip in MuonClip, then learns agentic skills from synthesized tasks and RL.

background.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models

further.title: GLM-5: from Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering
further.why: Long agent tasks make RL rollouts slow, so GLM-5 runs asynchronous RL that decouples rollouts from training.

main.title: The Big LLM Architecture Comparison
main.why: Open-weight LLMs differ in small but telling design details, and this article compares their architectures side by side, from DeepSeek V3 to Gemma 4.

main.title: DeepSeek-V4: Towards Highly Efficient Million-Token Context Intelligence
main.why: Attention cost grows with context length, so DeepSeek-V4 compresses and sparsifies attention, and adds hyper-connections and the Muon optimizer.

background.title: DeepSeek-V3.2: Pushing the Frontier of Open Large Language Models

further.title: Kimi Linear: An Expressive, Efficient Attention Architecture
Kimi K3 Technical Report
further.why: To add capacity at lower cost, Kimi K3 combines linear and full attention, attention residuals and a mixture of experts with many more experts.

further.title: On the Design of Qwen3.8-Next Architecture: Evaluation, Efficiency, and Training Stability
further.why: Architecture changes trade quality against cost and stability, so this paper judges a linear-attention hybrid, sparse attention and n-gram embeddings on each.

main.why: Post-training open models at scale is mostly an engineering problem, so Netflix built a framework covering loss masking, sequence packing and RL orchestration.
